lede: Feeds change shape: a column is added, a type changes, a new system renames things. A Delta table checks every write against its schema, so a mismatch stops the write instead of quietly spoiling the table. Then you decide how the schema should change.
objectives: Explain schema enforcement: what a Delta append accepts and what it refuses
Add a new column to a table with `mergeSchema`, and predict the values old rows get
Make a batch fit a table by renaming and casting to its exact types
Replace a table's schema on purpose with `overwriteSchema`, and know the limits of type widening

blocks.md:
`encounters` holds eight clinic visits. Three are from December 2025 and five from January 2026. On 1 January 2026 the feed started sending a new column, `discharge_disposition`: where the patient went after the visit.

The examples rebuild that history. First the table as it was in 2025, from the three oldest visits and four columns. A Delta table stores its schema in its transaction log, in the `metaData` entry (lesson 61).

blocks.title: The 2025 table
blocks.code:
cols = ["encounter_id", "patient_id", "encounter_class", "start_time"]
visits_2025 = encounters.orderBy("start_time").limit(3).select(cols)

path = "/tmp/clinic/encounters"
visits_2025.write.format("delta").save(path)

table = spark.read.format("delta").load(path)
table.printSchema()
print(table.count(), "visits")
blocks.note: `orderBy("start_time").limit(3)` picks the three December visits. The table's schema is the DataFrame's: four columns.

blocks.md: Plain Parquet files accept whatever you write next to them, and readers find out later. Delta checks first. That is **schema enforcement**: an append whose columns or types don't fit the table's schema is refused, and nothing is written.

blocks.title: A batch with a new column
blocks.note: The five 2026 visits carry `discharge_disposition`, which the table doesn't have. The full message prints both schemas and names the option that allows the change. The table ID in it is different on every run.

blocks.md: When the new column is wanted, say so: `.option("mergeSchema", "true")` on the append. Delta adds the batch's new columns to the table's schema, **at the end**, and writes the batch. Rows written before have no value for the new column, so they read as NULL. Nothing is rewritten: the old files stay as they were.

blocks.title: Add the column with mergeSchema
blocks.code:
cols = ["encounter_id", "patient_id", "encounter_class", "start_time"]
path = "/tmp/clinic/encounters"
encounters.orderBy("start_time").limit(3).select(cols).write.format("delta").save(path)

visits_2026 = encounters.orderBy("start_time", ascending=False).limit(5).select(cols + ["discharge_disposition"])
visits_2026.write.format("delta").mode("append").option("mergeSchema", "true").save(path)

table = spark.read.format("delta").load(path)
print(table.columns)
table.orderBy("start_time").show()
blocks.note: The three 2025 visits read NULL for the new column. Two 2026 visits are NULL too, for a different reason: telehealth visits never have a disposition.

blocks.md:
Two things that look like mismatches are fine:

- **Column order.** Delta matches an append's columns to the table's by name, not position.
- **A missing column.** A batch that lacks one of the table's columns is accepted; that column is NULL for its rows. Data from an old system that never had the column can still be appended.

blocks.title: A late visit from the old system
blocks.code:
from datetime import datetime

cols = ["encounter_id", "patient_id", "encounter_class", "start_time"]
path = "/tmp/clinic/encounters"
encounters.orderBy("start_time").limit(3).select(cols).write.format("delta").save(path)
visits_2026 = encounters.orderBy("start_time", ascending=False).limit(5).select(cols + ["discharge_disposition"])
visits_2026.write.format("delta").mode("append").option("mergeSchema", "true").save(path)

late = spark.createDataFrame(
    [(datetime(2025, 12, 29, 9, 30), "ambulatory", "PAT00006", "ENC000009")],
    "start_time TIMESTAMP, encounter_class STRING, patient_id STRING, encounter_id STRING",
)
late.write.format("delta").mode("append").save(path)

table = spark.read.format("delta").load(path)
print(table.columns)
table.orderBy("start_time").show()
blocks.note: The late visit's columns come in another order and without `discharge_disposition`. No option is needed: it's matched by name and gets NULL.

blocks.md: Types are checked strictly. Here `claims` stores its amounts as `decimal(12,2)`, and a partner sends them as doubles. `mergeSchema` adds columns, but it doesn't change a column's type, so it doesn't help.

blocks.title: An amount of the wrong type
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

path = "/tmp/clinic/claims"
claims.select("claim_id", "billed_amount", "paid_amount").write.format("delta").save(path)

partner = claims.select("claim_id", F.col("billed_amount").cast("double").alias("billed_amount"), "paid_amount")
partner.write.format("delta").mode("append").option("mergeSchema", "true").save(path)
blocks.note: Delta can't merge a double into a `decimal(12,2)` column, so it refuses even with `mergeSchema`.

blocks.md:
Make the batch fit instead: cast each column to the table's **exact** type (lesson 14) and give it the table's name. Exact really means exact. In this environment, an `int` batch into a `bigint` column and a `decimal(10,2)` into a `decimal(12,2)` column are both refused. Only very small integers (`tinyint`, `smallint`) go into an `int` column without a cast.

Delta can widen a column's type, if the table allows it: the table property `delta.enableTypeWidening` lets a `mergeSchema` append widen `int` to `bigint`, for example. It only ever widens. A number never narrows, and text never becomes a number.

blocks.title: Cast to fit, or let the table widen
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

path = "/tmp/clinic/claims"
claims.select("claim_id", "billed_amount", "paid_amount").write.format("delta").save(path)
print(dict(spark.read.format("delta").load(path).dtypes))

partner = claims.select("claim_id", F.col("billed_amount").cast("double").alias("billed_amount"), "paid_amount")
fixed = partner.select("claim_id", F.col("billed_amount").cast("decimal(12,2)").alias("billed_amount"), "paid_amount")
fixed.write.format("delta").mode("append").save(path)
print(spark.read.format("delta").load(path).count(), "claims")

bigger = spark.createDataFrame([("PAT00002", 3)], "patient_id STRING, visits BIGINT")
for widening in ["false", "true"]:
    counts = "/tmp/clinic/visit_counts_" + widening
    first = spark.createDataFrame([("PAT00001", 2)], "patient_id STRING, visits INT")
    first.write.format("delta").option("delta.enableTypeWidening", widening).save(counts)
    try:
        bigger.write.format("delta").mode("append").option("mergeSchema", "true").save(counts)
        print("widening", widening, "->", dict(spark.read.format("delta").load(counts).dtypes)["visits"])
    except Exception as e:
        print("widening", widening, "-> refused:", type(e).__name__)
blocks.note: After the cast, the partner's seven claims append to the seven already there. In the second part, an `int` column refuses a `bigint` batch, even with `mergeSchema`. A table created with `delta.enableTypeWidening` set to `true` accepts it, and the column becomes `bigint`.

blocks.md: Sometimes you want a different schema altogether: columns dropped, renamed or retyped. An append can't do that, and a plain `overwrite` replaces the rows but **keeps the old schema**. Add `.option("overwriteSchema", "true")` to an overwrite to replace the schema too. Use it on purpose: it's the one write that can silently remove columns other jobs read.

blocks.title: overwrite keeps the schema, overwriteSchema replaces it
blocks.code:
cols = ["encounter_id", "patient_id", "encounter_class", "start_time"]
path = "/tmp/clinic/encounters"
encounters.orderBy("start_time").limit(3).select(cols).write.format("delta").save(path)

encounters.select("encounter_id", "patient_id").write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").save(path)
print("overwrite:      ", spark.read.format("delta").load(path).columns)

encounters.select("encounter_id", "reason").write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").option("overwriteSchema", "true").save(path)
print("overwriteSchema:", spark.read.format("delta").load(path).columns)
blocks.note: The plain overwrite wrote two columns, but the table still has four; the other two are NULL now. With `overwriteSchema` the table has exactly the new DataFrame's columns.

concept.prompt: A Delta table has columns `a` and `b`. You append a batch with `a`, `b` and `c`, without any option. What happens?
choices: The batch is appended and `c` is dropped
The append is refused and nothing is written
The table is replaced by the batch
concept.why: Schema enforcement refuses a write whose schema doesn't fit. Add `mergeSchema` to add `c`.

concept.prompt: You append the 2026 visits with `mergeSchema`, adding `discharge_disposition`. What do the 2025 visits show in that column?
choices: The value of the first 2026 visit
The append fails because they have no value
concept.why: The old rows' files are not rewritten. They have no value for the new column, so they read as NULL.

concept.prompt: A table's `billed_amount` is `decimal(12,2)`. A batch has it as a double. Which write works?
choices: Append the batch as it is
concept.why: Delta checks types exactly, and `mergeSchema` doesn't change an existing column's type. Only the table's exact type is accepted.

review: A Delta table keeps its schema in its log and checks every write against it: a mismatch is refused, not written.
Columns are matched by name; a missing column becomes NULL, but an extra column is refused.
`mergeSchema` on an append adds the batch's new columns at the end; older rows read NULL there.
`mergeSchema` doesn't change types. Cast and rename the batch to the table's exact names and types.
With `delta.enableTypeWidening`, a `mergeSchema` append can widen a type such as `int` to `bigint`, never narrow it.
A plain `overwrite` keeps the table's schema; `overwriteSchema` replaces it.
